# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist - UP MAGAZINE


# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
#### Written by Leigh Pennington
##### _Published on April 22nd, 2025_
The renaissance man is one of many talents, proficient in multiple artistic avenues that often support one another in progression, knowledge, and execution. Oftentimes the creation of art, music, fashion and other sensory expressions hold the hands of one another, elevate and influence outcome, changing the scope of a cultural landscape. Another manner of understanding the qualities of the renaissance man is to look into the concept of whole-brain thinkers, those that consume and apply new information or skills by using both cognitive as well as creative functions, the left and right side of the brain working in tandem. These individuals are constant intake learners, able to absorb and utilize what resonates with the distinction of their nature.
Born in Harlem and raised in Clinton Hill, SMURFO grew up around the corner from Pratt University. This had a large influence on his childhood years and early progression as an artist. “I was able to go in there as a 12, 13 year old and do the summer camp there…I had already been drawing my whole life up until then, and no real drawing classes in my school, because it was a Catholic school…I remember just seeing the abundance of paints and the abundance of markers and supplies and easels. It really just struck something in me right before getting into high school, to go into art and design.
While in middle school he began his artistic experimentation with cartoons and drawings from television series like Cartoon Network’s Toonami, as well as crafting his own hybrid animal figures. At age 15 SMURFO decided to engage with drawing human figures, seeing it more often in his high school. While at the High School of Art and Design, graffiti came into his line of sight, noticing a great deal of the upperclassmen who were engaging in graffiti activities. “Coming from Catholic school, nobody was a graffiti writer, and I didn’t grow up around any of them personally. Then I got into high school and saw what was for real, in the New York street way, not in a cartoony way. Not drawing that weird “S” you’d see in high school bathrooms…I started practicing graffiti right then and there…Then started hitting streets right around 16 years old after a year of practicing my tag, once I finally came to SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others. Tagging with experienced peers around his own age encouraged SMURFO to take chances and inspired him to uptick his graffiti practice. “We all had left school one day, me and a bunch of other writers…we went to the Maspeth to hit freights. That’s when I caught a real bug for it, because that was my first time doing stuff illegally to that capacity. Like 10 of us….cutting school, hitting the yard up and down, and getting back to school before 3pm like rockstars, hyped the fuck up. That’s what really put the battery in my back. And that’s when I started hitting the streets and hitting Midtown and SOHO and Bed Stuy and Clinton Hill and Bushwick and everywhere I basically would go. I would catch a tag or several.”
As SMURFO continued to tag and paint he did so primarily on solo runs, gathering knowledge, experiencing his first official arrest, and developing his own methodology of tag placement and style. “I found it easier to just go up by myself. I started painting in the daytime for the first time, just realizing you know what to look out for and what not to look out for…After the first time I got caught for graffiti, I had done three nights in bookings my first night and got a crash course on everything at once from boofing drugs and money to standing your ground to police misconduct…After I got out I was like, I think I’m cool to keep doing this haha jail was a different story. I didn’t get put off or scared by central bookings. It was just protocol for a while until I really learned the game. I’ve been writing for 15 years plus since then.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate. He has always been mindful of the ethics of graffiti, while aiming with his work to make a lasting and outright impression by strategically placing his tags. “It’s always been just catching where I fit. That’s what I love. I love graffiti where I take spots that nobody even thinks about, but it always catches your eye. I always took my approach to graffiti as if you’re just looking and you’re catching everything in your peripheral, and everything straight on, and stuff beneath you and stuff above you all in the same eye vision. So if I catch a tag somewhere with a certain color, it just pops. You know, you’re gonna see it regardless if you were looking for it. It commands attention.”
Maintaining his approach with tagging, SMURFO also enjoys leaving cognitive messages out on the streets. These phrases are the artist’s way of being in dialogue with the greater public, something that, “would prompt somebody to either have a moment of self reflection, or a moment of realizing a truth that they might not have wanted to accept before…I like to write it in a way where it’s going to touch everybody.” While most of his messages are inherently positive, he does not shy away from public reminders of the need for understanding the dichotomy between moments of strength as well as weakness. “You look in the mirror and see if this applies to you. I’m only doing that because I’ve had to ask myself the same question.” One of his favorites is writing on discarded mirrors, “TAKE A DEEP LOOK AT YOURSELF – SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
During COVID he completed a wall in the basement of a South Williamsburg Establishment bestowed with the prompt “Before they can fuck with you, you have to fuck with you.” This philosophy is a pointed message for humanity, the mental acuity needed to push one’s aspirations to the next level in an earnest, authentic, and yet humble manner. He expounded, “No matter what that mission is you have to be so unequivocally about it that people respect that, and then, therefore can respect you. But if you’re doing anything without your full intent, people are going to catch that whether it be for money or clout or a narcissistic need for spotlight…When it comes to graffiti especially, you definitely want people to realize that you’re about what you’re putting out…I’m constantly struggling with my own life as an artist, you know, being able to say that I’m proud of myself and my intentions and not be boastful and being able to self – actualize and reflect without self loathing.”
SMURFO has also added these phrases to clothing. His first job in the city was doing airbrush sneakers, hats, canvases, jackets, shoes etc. on the South Street Seaport starting in 2006. He was there from the time he left high school till 2013. “So I got a lot of my skills that I use now from there and I was doing custom clothing that whole time, not many people were doing it. It was a lil out of style by that time for NYC.” Currently SMURFO has his own brand of hand-designed garments, Steady Handed Hooligans, that pay homage to his defined painting as well as sketch book style, which is most often, similar to his quotes, a means of social commentary or public engagement in self-reflexivity.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters. Some of these he translates from paper onto walls. His murals have a distinct cartoon style, however the appearance of characters designed by the artist carries within it something mischievous, naughty, yet wholly charming. As a whole-brain thinker, his inspiration for his animated personas are inspired by a multitude of illustrators. “There’s all these sub genres of art that are huge and they relate to everything in the grand lexicon… I love that comic book art style. I love that realistic style. I love that very heavily cross hatched shaded cartoon style that’s still realistic like Robert Crumb does. So I get my inspiration from a lot of different sources, and then, I could put them all together.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters.
One of his most known characters goes by the name of Roscoe the Rat. An icon of New York, the rat is resourceful, independent, adorable, and somewhat of a tricky motherfucker. However he is wholly lovable. In 2021, SMURFO completed a mural on East Houston proclaiming the season of the rat to be in full swing. There are numerous versions of Roscoe included in the work, some clad with a roguish face, others gazing in adoration at the central figure, the main Roscoe who is throwing up his own “Roscoe the Rat” tag. The piece can be construed as a larger metaphor for NYC come the springtime. In many ways we are all Roscoe the Rat when we emerge from the winter hibernation of our apartments. Ready to smell the fresh air, make seemingly “bad decisions”, and rekindle with faces perhaps we have not seen in awhile. Roscoe isn’t so much an alter ego for SMURFO as he is an alternate state of mind.
While many of his walls are located within New York, SMURFO has completed walls internationally, bringing his singular execution to everything from bank gates to elementary schools. In 2023 SMURFO was invited by his friend Chef G to complete his most recent international mural in Thessaloniki, Greece. Here we see his particular style projected onto human figures and expressions. “We put together this gig where I would DJ after doing this big mural while everybody was kind of sitting down, drinking their coffees and drinking their beers or whatever… My inspo for it was just the faces that I would see in Greece. So it’s a lot of immigrants, it’s a lot of mixed race Europeans. It’s a lot of everybody.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities. While staying in Aspra Spitia,SMURFO was commissioned to paint a larger mural, three whole walls, for a school in a small village of only 3000 people, “just to say thank you to the village I was staying in while I was out there… just for the kids. Its so beautiful there, kissed by God, I wanted those kids to say they had an artist from New York City come and do that for them. And I wanted to say I did that for the community. So I was super proud of that one.”
More recently SMURFO has begun to shy away from adhering to strictly cartoon style walls. The last few years he has started to experiment more with realism by playing with different materials, layering patterns, and visual topics. “For a very long time, I was very one sided with the cartooning, just because I didn’t have the patience to draw realistically. The older I get as an artist, art becomes more therapeutic…I actually love to sit there and draw realistically now and mix in that part of me that was younger…my old style and my new style. It’s not even just the new style, it’s just me becoming more patient with my work….new elements, elements taken out, and then some pieces I like to do where all of it is encompassing…where it looks like organized chaos, is the challenge for me, and that’s what I like.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
This evolution can be seen in many of his works on canvas. One of his largest commissioned pieces to date, two canvases filled to the brim with life and color, is definitively more adventurous. The works are a combination of all his recent styles, playing with heightened as well as defined shapes and characters. To achieve this look SMURFO uses “spray paint, acrylic, a little bit of oil stick, charcoal, color pencil, everything…I’ve been getting good at figuring out how to get a little bit of an oil aesthetic with acrylic. So now it’s just mastering the materials that I always use, and it’s always something to learn. I’m constantly putting things together whether I think they should match or not, just to see the effect I get…and seeing how I use all that to my advantage.”
One of his other works on canvas entitled “1989” is a layered collection of visuals and dramatic personas from the year of his birth. Disney characters, anime and street style figures all collected and displayed in a kaleidoscope of vibrant hues and texture. Many of SMURFO’s works can be viewed as archives of culture, a noted and deliberate observation and conservation of artistic endeavours passed but never forgotten, always influential. This trait also comes across in spades within he work as a DJ, an “heir to the vibes.”
Similar to art, music has always been a central component of SMURFO’s world. During our interview I was pleasantly stunned to learn he hails from jazz and funk royalty. His grandmother is Terry Pollard (Queen of the Vibes) one of the first African American women to play on syndicated television. She performed on NBC’s Tonight starring Steve Allen in 1956, performing with the Terry Gibbs quartet. Her son, SMURFO’s father, is Dennis Weeden who aided in the founding of P-Funk out of Detroit along with George Clinton, Bootsy Collins, and Amp Fiddler (RIP). When SMURFO was born, his father was hitting the height of career. “I had funk music playing in my house all the time. So I was growing up with that vibration constantly all through my upbringing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Inspired by the emerging DJ culture of the mid-2000s, SMURFO began his music career managing a cohort of DJs known as the WC Kids (Wild Crazy Kids). “My boy Atiba and my boy Matthew from high school, we started doing our own parties at Matt’s house. They bought a setup and from then on, we just did parties every few weeks at the height of Facebook and Youtube just popping off. There was still no Instagram hahaha…I was on the mic at first, so I was always talking shit and controlling the vibe.” As the parties began to attract bigger and bigger crowds (Webster Hall, Bowery Ballroom, Gramercy theater) SMURFO began contemplating stepping into the booth on his own to see what he could create. “At some point I said, Okay, I have all this music knowledge, because as much as they were downloading and getting sets ready, I was doing the same thing all the time, but I wasn’t DJing. So I said, Okay, I gotta figure it out. How am I gonna DJ myself?”
SMURFO started his solo DJ career at Local 138 in the Lower East Side. His bartender at the spot, Aaron McCann, one of the great owners of Williamsburg Pizza bought him a computer for cheap, and for nearly eight years from that time he had a residency every Thursday night at the location. The motto was ‘HIP HOP, HOUSE AND HOT SHIT’. DJing for SMURFO held a substantial goal of civic responsibility and engagement. “DJing was the thing I did for the people because I knew I could pilot. Art was the thing I always did for myself first…From the beginning, I always wanted people to catch a little bit of a history lesson the way I had grown up with. So if I know people don’t really get to hear funk music or disco or house music or new wave or Soul the way I love to hear it, then I’m gonna put that in my set…you can’t have the one without the other. There is no top Hip Hop track of 2013 without that top track from 1985.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another. The album art he was surrounded by in his youth was his first education in the combined power of audio visual technique and synchronicity. “From seeing all my dad’s old album covers, yeah, looking at that artwork, I was like, Oh, okay, this is sick…The album artwork of the 80s and 90s is just insane…some of it’s really intricate, and it’s all hand done, no, digital, no, AI…That’s when I started learning about artwork matching a vibration… I would say that the music definitely helped with my artwork in a lot of ways, but it came later on in life. I noticed it when I was young. It didn’t really start to hit me till I got into my 30s…you know, having an artist listen to an album and paint and draw depending on what they’re hearing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another.
SMURFO is a whole-brain artist. Over the course of his life he has listened and learned from his surroundings, never fearful of the intertwined phases of his artistic endeavors which has grown to encompass graffiti, music, fashion and so much more. SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher. His visual works and music possess either a great deal of forethought or exact improvisation. Regardless, his mental acuity, intentionality, and originality has become refined throughout the history of his career.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher.
To finish our interview, he provided an additional piece of wisdom for the upcoming generations of artists that in many ways defines his own journey. “I would only want to tell the new generation of painters and artists who are doing what they love to do to just stick with it…everybody’s style has to sharpen up. You know you can’t be as rough as you were five years ago, five years later. You’re gonna have to make sure that you are always keeping your work tight. So do not be afraid to improve. Just because you feel like this one aesthetic you have is going to be the thing, and that might counteract me saying, do what you love to do, but I’m saying don’t be afraid to do it even better or to trim the fat.”

## Peyo
Pierre Culliford (known as Peyo) was born in Brussels on 25 June 1928.
He started his working life at the age of 15. He began as a cinema projectionist, and then went to work in an animation studio. The studio closed down and Peyo decided to focus on cartoon comic strips. These were published in various daily newspapers, but the early days were difficult.
It was not until he joined the magazine Spirou that he found success with Johan & Peewit. And it was as part of this series that he created the Smurfs.
Following their appearance, Peyo continued working on the adventures of Johan & Peewit and of Pussy the cat. He also created Benoît Brisefer (later Benny Breakiron), an extraordinarily strong little boy. But eventually the worldwide success of the Smurfs consumed all his energy. And he dedicated himself fully to their epic story, in all its aspects, until his death in 1992.
Peyo said : « As a boy, I loved to draw... But in fact, all children draw; some of them decide to become adults, serious people, and then there are others who refuse to make the transition and who create cartoon characters. »
The qualities he possessed and that contributed to his art, his success and timeless work were: clear narration, humour full of poetry, a strong graphic style and constant creativity... Not forgetting values that transcend generations such as tolerance, faith in the future and respect for others.
Today, Peyo’s family and staff continue his work in the same spirit.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
#### Written by Leigh Pennington
##### _Published on April 22nd, 2025_
The renaissance man is one of many talents, proficient in multiple artistic avenues that often support one another in progression, knowledge, and execution. Oftentimes the creation of art, music, fashion and other sensory expressions hold the hands of one another, elevate and influence outcome, changing the scope of a cultural landscape. Another manner of understanding the qualities of the renaissance man is to look into the concept of whole-brain thinkers, those that consume and apply new information or skills by using both cognitive as well as creative functions, the left and right side of the brain working in tandem. These individuals are constant intake learners, able to absorb and utilize what resonates with the distinction of their nature.
Born in Harlem and raised in Clinton Hill, SMURFO grew up around the corner from Pratt University. This had a large influence on his childhood years and early progression as an artist. “I was able to go in there as a 12, 13 year old and do the summer camp there…I had already been drawing my whole life up until then, and no real drawing classes in my school, because it was a Catholic school…I remember just seeing the abundance of paints and the abundance of markers and supplies and easels. It really just struck something in me right before getting into high school, to go into art and design.
While in middle school he began his artistic experimentation with cartoons and drawings from television series like Cartoon Network’s Toonami, as well as crafting his own hybrid animal figures. At age 15 SMURFO decided to engage with drawing human figures, seeing it more often in his high school. While at the High School of Art and Design, graffiti came into his line of sight, noticing a great deal of the upperclassmen who were engaging in graffiti activities. “Coming from Catholic school, nobody was a graffiti writer, and I didn’t grow up around any of them personally. Then I got into high school and saw what was for real, in the New York street way, not in a cartoony way. Not drawing that weird “S” you’d see in high school bathrooms…I started practicing graffiti right then and there…Then started hitting streets right around 16 years old after a year of practicing my tag, once I finally came to SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others. Tagging with experienced peers around his own age encouraged SMURFO to take chances and inspired him to uptick his graffiti practice. “We all had left school one day, me and a bunch of other writers…we went to the Maspeth to hit freights. That’s when I caught a real bug for it, because that was my first time doing stuff illegally to that capacity. Like 10 of us….cutting school, hitting the yard up and down, and getting back to school before 3pm like rockstars, hyped the fuck up. That’s what really put the battery in my back. And that’s when I started hitting the streets and hitting Midtown and SOHO and Bed Stuy and Clinton Hill and Bushwick and everywhere I basically would go. I would catch a tag or several.”
As SMURFO continued to tag and paint he did so primarily on solo runs, gathering knowledge, experiencing his first official arrest, and developing his own methodology of tag placement and style. “I found it easier to just go up by myself. I started painting in the daytime for the first time, just realizing you know what to look out for and what not to look out for…After the first time I got caught for graffiti, I had done three nights in bookings my first night and got a crash course on everything at once from boofing drugs and money to standing your ground to police misconduct…After I got out I was like, I think I’m cool to keep doing this haha jail was a different story. I didn’t get put off or scared by central bookings. It was just protocol for a while until I really learned the game. I’ve been writing for 15 years plus since then.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate. He has always been mindful of the ethics of graffiti, while aiming with his work to make a lasting and outright impression by strategically placing his tags. “It’s always been just catching where I fit. That’s what I love. I love graffiti where I take spots that nobody even thinks about, but it always catches your eye. I always took my approach to graffiti as if you’re just looking and you’re catching everything in your peripheral, and everything straight on, and stuff beneath you and stuff above you all in the same eye vision. So if I catch a tag somewhere with a certain color, it just pops. You know, you’re gonna see it regardless if you were looking for it. It commands attention.”
Maintaining his approach with tagging, SMURFO also enjoys leaving cognitive messages out on the streets. These phrases are the artist’s way of being in dialogue with the greater public, something that, “would prompt somebody to either have a moment of self reflection, or a moment of realizing a truth that they might not have wanted to accept before…I like to write it in a way where it’s going to touch everybody.” While most of his messages are inherently positive, he does not shy away from public reminders of the need for understanding the dichotomy between moments of strength as well as weakness. “You look in the mirror and see if this applies to you. I’m only doing that because I’ve had to ask myself the same question.” One of his favorites is writing on discarded mirrors, “TAKE A DEEP LOOK AT YOURSELF – SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
During COVID he completed a wall in the basement of a South Williamsburg Establishment bestowed with the prompt “Before they can fuck with you, you have to fuck with you.” This philosophy is a pointed message for humanity, the mental acuity needed to push one’s aspirations to the next level in an earnest, authentic, and yet humble manner. He expounded, “No matter what that mission is you have to be so unequivocally about it that people respect that, and then, therefore can respect you. But if you’re doing anything without your full intent, people are going to catch that whether it be for money or clout or a narcissistic need for spotlight…When it comes to graffiti especially, you definitely want people to realize that you’re about what you’re putting out…I’m constantly struggling with my own life as an artist, you know, being able to say that I’m proud of myself and my intentions and not be boastful and being able to self – actualize and reflect without self loathing.”
SMURFO has also added these phrases to clothing. His first job in the city was doing airbrush sneakers, hats, canvases, jackets, shoes etc. on the South Street Seaport starting in 2006. He was there from the time he left high school till 2013. “So I got a lot of my skills that I use now from there and I was doing custom clothing that whole time, not many people were doing it. It was a lil out of style by that time for NYC.” Currently SMURFO has his own brand of hand-designed garments, Steady Handed Hooligans, that pay homage to his defined painting as well as sketch book style, which is most often, similar to his quotes, a means of social commentary or public engagement in self-reflexivity.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters. Some of these he translates from paper onto walls. His murals have a distinct cartoon style, however the appearance of characters designed by the artist carries within it something mischievous, naughty, yet wholly charming. As a whole-brain thinker, his inspiration for his animated personas are inspired by a multitude of illustrators. “There’s all these sub genres of art that are huge and they relate to everything in the grand lexicon… I love that comic book art style. I love that realistic style. I love that very heavily cross hatched shaded cartoon style that’s still realistic like Robert Crumb does. So I get my inspiration from a lot of different sources, and then, I could put them all together.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters.
One of his most known characters goes by the name of Roscoe the Rat. An icon of New York, the rat is resourceful, independent, adorable, and somewhat of a tricky motherfucker. However he is wholly lovable. In 2021, SMURFO completed a mural on East Houston proclaiming the season of the rat to be in full swing. There are numerous versions of Roscoe included in the work, some clad with a roguish face, others gazing in adoration at the central figure, the main Roscoe who is throwing up his own “Roscoe the Rat” tag. The piece can be construed as a larger metaphor for NYC come the springtime. In many ways we are all Roscoe the Rat when we emerge from the winter hibernation of our apartments. Ready to smell the fresh air, make seemingly “bad decisions”, and rekindle with faces perhaps we have not seen in awhile. Roscoe isn’t so much an alter ego for SMURFO as he is an alternate state of mind.
While many of his walls are located within New York, SMURFO has completed walls internationally, bringing his singular execution to everything from bank gates to elementary schools. In 2023 SMURFO was invited by his friend Chef G to complete his most recent international mural in Thessaloniki, Greece. Here we see his particular style projected onto human figures and expressions. “We put together this gig where I would DJ after doing this big mural while everybody was kind of sitting down, drinking their coffees and drinking their beers or whatever… My inspo for it was just the faces that I would see in Greece. So it’s a lot of immigrants, it’s a lot of mixed race Europeans. It’s a lot of everybody.”
texts.7:
# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities. While staying in Aspra Spitia,SMURFO was commissioned to paint a larger mural, three whole walls, for a school in a small village of only 3000 people, “just to say thank you to the village I was staying in while I was out there… just for the kids. Its so beautiful there, kissed by God, I wanted those kids to say they had an artist from New York City come and do that for them. And I wanted to say I did that for the community. So I was super proud of that one.”
More recently SMURFO has begun to shy away from adhering to strictly cartoon style walls. The last few years he has started to experiment more with realism by playing with different materials, layering patterns, and visual topics. “For a very long time, I was very one sided with the cartooning, just because I didn’t have the patience to draw realistically. The older I get as an artist, art becomes more therapeutic…I actually love to sit there and draw realistically now and mix in that part of me that was younger…my old style and my new style. It’s not even just the new style, it’s just me becoming more patient with my work….new elements, elements taken out, and then some pieces I like to do where all of it is encompassing…where it looks like organized chaos, is the challenge for me, and that’s what I like.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
This evolution can be seen in many of his works on canvas. One of his largest commissioned pieces to date, two canvases filled to the brim with life and color, is definitively more adventurous. The works are a combination of all his recent styles, playing with heightened as well as defined shapes and characters. To achieve this look SMURFO uses “spray paint, acrylic, a little bit of oil stick, charcoal, color pencil, everything…I’ve been getting good at figuring out how to get a little bit of an oil aesthetic with acrylic. So now it’s just mastering the materials that I always use, and it’s always something to learn. I’m constantly putting things together whether I think they should match or not, just to see the effect I get…and seeing how I use all that to my advantage.”
One of his other works on canvas entitled “1989” is a layered collection of visuals and dramatic personas from the year of his birth. Disney characters, anime and street style figures all collected and displayed in a kaleidoscope of vibrant hues and texture. Many of SMURFO’s works can be viewed as archives of culture, a noted and deliberate observation and conservation of artistic endeavours passed but never forgotten, always influential. This trait also comes across in spades within he work as a DJ, an “heir to the vibes.”
Similar to art, music has always been a central component of SMURFO’s world. During our interview I was pleasantly stunned to learn he hails from jazz and funk royalty. His grandmother is Terry Pollard (Queen of the Vibes) one of the first African American women to play on syndicated television. She performed on NBC’s Tonight starring Steve Allen in 1956, performing with the Terry Gibbs quartet. Her son, SMURFO’s father, is Dennis Weeden who aided in the founding of P-Funk out of Detroit along with George Clinton, Bootsy Collins, and Amp Fiddler (RIP). When SMURFO was born, his father was hitting the height of career. “I had funk music playing in my house all the time. So I was growing up with that vibration constantly all through my upbringing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Inspired by the emerging DJ culture of the mid-2000s, SMURFO began his music career managing a cohort of DJs known as the WC Kids (Wild Crazy Kids). “My boy Atiba and my boy Matthew from high school, we started doing our own parties at Matt’s house. They bought a setup and from then on, we just did parties every few weeks at the height of Facebook and Youtube just popping off. There was still no Instagram hahaha…I was on the mic at first, so I was always talking shit and controlling the vibe.” As the parties began to attract bigger and bigger crowds (Webster Hall, Bowery Ballroom, Gramercy theater) SMURFO began contemplating stepping into the booth on his own to see what he could create. “At some point I said, Okay, I have all this music knowledge, because as much as they were downloading and getting sets ready, I was doing the same thing all the time, but I wasn’t DJing. So I said, Okay, I gotta figure it out. How am I gonna DJ myself?”
SMURFO started his solo DJ career at Local 138 in the Lower East Side. His bartender at the spot, Aaron McCann, one of the great owners of Williamsburg Pizza bought him a computer for cheap, and for nearly eight years from that time he had a residency every Thursday night at the location. The motto was ‘HIP HOP, HOUSE AND HOT SHIT’. DJing for SMURFO held a substantial goal of civic responsibility and engagement. “DJing was the thing I did for the people because I knew I could pilot. Art was the thing I always did for myself first…From the beginning, I always wanted people to catch a little bit of a history lesson the way I had grown up with. So if I know people don’t really get to hear funk music or disco or house music or new wave or Soul the way I love to hear it, then I’m gonna put that in my set…you can’t have the one without the other. There is no top Hip Hop track of 2013 without that top track from 1985.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another. The album art he was surrounded by in his youth was his first education in the combined power of audio visual technique and synchronicity. “From seeing all my dad’s old album covers, yeah, looking at that artwork, I was like, Oh, okay, this is sick…The album artwork of the 80s and 90s is just insane…some of it’s really intricate, and it’s all hand done, no, digital, no, AI…That’s when I started learning about artwork matching a vibration… I would say that the music definitely helped with my artwork in a lot of ways, but it came later on in life. I noticed it when I was young. It didn’t really start to hit me till I got into my 30s…you know, having an artist listen to an album and paint and draw depending on what they’re hearing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another.
SMURFO is a whole-brain artist. Over the course of his life he has listened and learned from his surroundings, never fearful of the intertwined phases of his artistic endeavors which has grown to encompass graffiti, music, fashion and so much more. SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher. His visual works and music possess either a great deal of forethought or exact improvisation. Regardless, his mental acuity, intentionality, and originality has become refined throughout the history of his career.
texts.12:
# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher.
To finish our interview, he provided an additional piece of wisdom for the upcoming generations of artists that in many ways defines his own journey. “I would only want to tell the new generation of painters and artists who are doing what they love to do to just stick with it…everybody’s style has to sharpen up. You know you can’t be as rough as you were five years ago, five years later. You’re gonna have to make sure that you are always keeping your work tight. So do not be afraid to improve. Just because you feel like this one aesthetic you have is going to be the thing, and that might counteract me saying, do what you love to do, but I’m saying don’t be afraid to do it even better or to trim the fat.”

It really just struck something in me right before getting into high school, to go into art and design.
While in middle school he began his artistic experimentation with cartoons and drawings from television series like Cartoon Network’s Toonami, as well as crafting his own hybrid animal figures. At age 15 SMURFO decided to engage with drawing human figures, seeing it more often in his high school. While at the High School of Art and Design, graffiti came into his line of sight, noticing a great deal of the upperclassmen who were engaging in graffiti activities. “Coming from Catholic school, nobody was a graffiti writer, and I didn’t grow up around any of them personally. Then I got into high school and saw what was for real, in the New York street way, not in a cartoony way. Not drawing that weird “S” you’d see in high school bathrooms…I started practicing graffiti right then and there…Then started hitting streets right around 16 years old after a year of practicing my tag, once I finally came to SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others. Tagging with experienced peers around his own age encouraged SMURFO to take chances and inspired him to uptick his graffiti practice. “We all had left school one day, me and a bunch of other writers…we went to the Maspeth to hit freights. That’s when I caught a real bug for it, because that was my first time doing stuff illegally to that capacity. Like 10 of us….cutting school, hitting the yard up and down, and getting back to school before 3pm like rockstars, hyped the fuck up. That’s what really put the battery in my back. And that’s when I started hitting the streets and hitting Midtown and SOHO and Bed Stuy and Clinton Hill and Bushwick and everywhere I basically would go. I would catch a tag or several.”
As SMURFO continued to tag and paint he did so primarily on solo runs, gathering knowledge, experiencing his first official arrest, and developing his own methodology of tag placement and style. “I found it easier to just go up by myself. I started painting in the daytime for the first time, just realizing you know what to look out for and what not to look out for…After the first time I got caught for graffiti, I had done three nights in bookings my first night and got a crash course on everything at once from boofing drugs and money to standing your ground to police misconduct…After I got out I was like, I think I’m cool to keep doing this haha jail was a different story. I didn’t get put off or scared by central bookings. It was just protocol for a while until I really learned the game. I’ve been writing for 15 years plus since then.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO practiced graffiti casually at first, throwing up small stickers and phrases where he felt comfortable. During his senior year however, his tagging activities escalated under the tutelage and watchful eyes of The Funk Squad, a crew of writers out of Queens that consisted of JAY2 (RIP), JADER, and TAKE2 amongst others.
SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate. He has always been mindful of the ethics of graffiti, while aiming with his work to make a lasting and outright impression by strategically placing his tags. “It’s always been just catching where I fit. That’s what I love. I love graffiti where I take spots that nobody even thinks about, but it always catches your eye. I always took my approach to graffiti as if you’re just looking and you’re catching everything in your peripheral, and everything straight on, and stuff beneath you and stuff above you all in the same eye vision. So if I catch a tag somewhere with a certain color, it just pops. You know, you’re gonna see it regardless if you were looking for it. It commands attention.”
Maintaining his approach with tagging, SMURFO also enjoys leaving cognitive messages out on the streets. These phrases are the artist’s way of being in dialogue with the greater public, something that, “would prompt somebody to either have a moment of self reflection, or a moment of realizing a truth that they might not have wanted to accept before…I like to write it in a way where it’s going to touch everybody.” While most of his messages are inherently positive, he does not shy away from public reminders of the need for understanding the dichotomy between moments of strength as well as weakness. “You look in the mirror and see if this applies to you. I’m only doing that because I’ve had to ask myself the same question.” One of his favorites is writing on discarded mirrors, “TAKE A DEEP LOOK AT YOURSELF – SMURFO.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
During COVID he completed a wall in the basement of a South Williamsburg Establishment bestowed with the prompt “Before they can fuck with you, you have to fuck with you.” This philosophy is a pointed message for humanity, the mental acuity needed to push one’s aspirations to the next level in an earnest, authentic, and yet humble manner. He expounded, “No matter what that mission is you have to be so unequivocally about it that people respect that, and then, therefore can respect you. But if you’re doing anything without your full intent, people are going to catch that whether it be for money or clout or a narcissistic need for spotlight…When it comes to graffiti especially, you definitely want people to realize that you’re about what you’re putting out…I’m constantly struggling with my own life as an artist, you know, being able to say that I’m proud of myself and my intentions and not be boastful and being able to self – actualize and reflect without self loathing.”
SMURFO has also added these phrases to clothing. His first job in the city was doing airbrush sneakers, hats, canvases, jackets, shoes etc. on the South Street Seaport starting in 2006. He was there from the time he left high school till 2013. “So I got a lot of my skills that I use now from there and I was doing custom clothing that whole time, not many people were doing it. It was a lil out of style by that time for NYC.” Currently SMURFO has his own brand of hand-designed garments, Steady Handed Hooligans, that pay homage to his defined painting as well as sketch book style, which is most often, similar to his quotes, a means of social commentary or public engagement in self-reflexivity.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO’s MO as a graffiti writer has prioritized tagging at an accelerated and honorable rate.
He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters. Some of these he translates from paper onto walls. His murals have a distinct cartoon style, however the appearance of characters designed by the artist carries within it something mischievous, naughty, yet wholly charming. As a whole-brain thinker, his inspiration for his animated personas are inspired by a multitude of illustrators. “There’s all these sub genres of art that are huge and they relate to everything in the grand lexicon… I love that comic book art style. I love that realistic style. I love that very heavily cross hatched shaded cartoon style that’s still realistic like Robert Crumb does. So I get my inspiration from a lot of different sources, and then, I could put them all together.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## He always has his sketchbook on hand, which is filled to the brim with entire theatricals of realistic as well as animated characters.
One of his most known characters goes by the name of Roscoe the Rat. An icon of New York, the rat is resourceful, independent, adorable, and somewhat of a tricky motherfucker. However he is wholly lovable. In 2021, SMURFO completed a mural on East Houston proclaiming the season of the rat to be in full swing. There are numerous versions of Roscoe included in the work, some clad with a roguish face, others gazing in adoration at the central figure, the main Roscoe who is throwing up his own “Roscoe the Rat” tag. The piece can be construed as a larger metaphor for NYC come the springtime. In many ways we are all Roscoe the Rat when we emerge from the winter hibernation of our apartments. Ready to smell the fresh air, make seemingly “bad decisions”, and rekindle with faces perhaps we have not seen in awhile. Roscoe isn’t so much an alter ego for SMURFO as he is an alternate state of mind.
While many of his walls are located within New York, SMURFO has completed walls internationally, bringing his singular execution to everything from bank gates to elementary schools. In 2023 SMURFO was invited by his friend Chef G to complete his most recent international mural in Thessaloniki, Greece. Here we see his particular style projected onto human figures and expressions. “We put together this gig where I would DJ after doing this big mural while everybody was kind of sitting down, drinking their coffees and drinking their beers or whatever… My inspo for it was just the faces that I would see in Greece. So it’s a lot of immigrants, it’s a lot of mixed race Europeans. It’s a lot of everybody.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities. While staying in Aspra Spitia,SMURFO was commissioned to paint a larger mural, three whole walls, for a school in a small village of only 3000 people, “just to say thank you to the village I was staying in while I was out there… just for the kids. Its so beautiful there, kissed by God, I wanted those kids to say they had an artist from New York City come and do that for them. And I wanted to say I did that for the community. So I was super proud of that one.”
More recently SMURFO has begun to shy away from adhering to strictly cartoon style walls. The last few years he has started to experiment more with realism by playing with different materials, layering patterns, and visual topics. “For a very long time, I was very one sided with the cartooning, just because I didn’t have the patience to draw realistically. The older I get as an artist, art becomes more therapeutic…I actually love to sit there and draw realistically now and mix in that part of me that was younger…my old style and my new style. It’s not even just the new style, it’s just me becoming more patient with my work….new elements, elements taken out, and then some pieces I like to do where all of it is encompassing…where it looks like organized chaos, is the challenge for me, and that’s what I like.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
This evolution can be seen in many of his works on canvas. One of his largest commissioned pieces to date, two canvases filled to the brim with life and color, is definitively more adventurous. The works are a combination of all his recent styles, playing with heightened as well as defined shapes and characters. To achieve this look SMURFO uses “spray paint, acrylic, a little bit of oil stick, charcoal, color pencil, everything…I’ve been getting good at figuring out how to get a little bit of an oil aesthetic with acrylic. So now it’s just mastering the materials that I always use, and it’s always something to learn. I’m constantly putting things together whether I think they should match or not, just to see the effect I get…and seeing how I use all that to my advantage.”
One of his other works on canvas entitled “1989” is a layered collection of visuals and dramatic personas from the year of his birth. Disney characters, anime and street style figures all collected and displayed in a kaleidoscope of vibrant hues and texture. Many of SMURFO’s works can be viewed as archives of culture, a noted and deliberate observation and conservation of artistic endeavours passed but never forgotten, always influential. This trait also comes across in spades within he work as a DJ, an “heir to the vibes.”
Similar to art, music has always been a central component of SMURFO’s world. During our interview I was pleasantly stunned to learn he hails from jazz and funk royalty. His grandmother is Terry Pollard (Queen of the Vibes) one of the first African American women to play on syndicated television. She performed on NBC’s Tonight starring Steve Allen in 1956, performing with the Terry Gibbs quartet. Her son, SMURFO’s father, is Dennis Weeden who aided in the founding of P-Funk out of Detroit along with George Clinton, Bootsy Collins, and Amp Fiddler (RIP). When SMURFO was born, his father was hitting the height of career. “I had funk music playing in my house all the time. So I was growing up with that vibration constantly all through my upbringing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
Inspired by the emerging DJ culture of the mid-2000s, SMURFO began his music career managing a cohort of DJs known as the WC Kids (Wild Crazy Kids). “My boy Atiba and my boy Matthew from high school, we started doing our own parties at Matt’s house. They bought a setup and from then on, we just did parties every few weeks at the height of Facebook and Youtube just popping off. There was still no Instagram hahaha…I was on the mic at first, so I was always talking shit and controlling the vibe.” As the parties began to attract bigger and bigger crowds (Webster Hall, Bowery Ballroom, Gramercy theater) SMURFO began contemplating stepping into the booth on his own to see what he could create. “At some point I said, Okay, I have all this music knowledge, because as much as they were downloading and getting sets ready, I was doing the same thing all the time, but I wasn’t DJing. So I said, Okay, I gotta figure it out. How am I gonna DJ myself?”
SMURFO started his solo DJ career at Local 138 in the Lower East Side. His bartender at the spot, Aaron McCann, one of the great owners of Williamsburg Pizza bought him a computer for cheap, and for nearly eight years from that time he had a residency every Thursday night at the location. The motto was ‘HIP HOP, HOUSE AND HOT SHIT’. DJing for SMURFO held a substantial goal of civic responsibility and engagement. “DJing was the thing I did for the people because I knew I could pilot. Art was the thing I always did for myself first…From the beginning, I always wanted people to catch a little bit of a history lesson the way I had grown up with. So if I know people don’t really get to hear funk music or disco or house music or new wave or Soul the way I love to hear it, then I’m gonna put that in my set…you can’t have the one without the other. There is no top Hip Hop track of 2013 without that top track from 1985.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## Exposure is important for the artist, however he also utilizes his work and talents to give back to communities
For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another. The album art he was surrounded by in his youth was his first education in the combined power of audio visual technique and synchronicity. “From seeing all my dad’s old album covers, yeah, looking at that artwork, I was like, Oh, okay, this is sick…The album artwork of the 80s and 90s is just insane…some of it’s really intricate, and it’s all hand done, no, digital, no, AI…That’s when I started learning about artwork matching a vibration… I would say that the music definitely helped with my artwork in a lot of ways, but it came later on in life. I noticed it when I was young. It didn’t really start to hit me till I got into my 30s…you know, having an artist listen to an album and paint and draw depending on what they’re hearing.”

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## For SMURFO music and art go hand in hand with their level of influence on one another.
SMURFO is a whole-brain artist. Over the course of his life he has listened and learned from his surroundings, never fearful of the intertwined phases of his artistic endeavors which has grown to encompass graffiti, music, fashion and so much more. SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher. His visual works and music possess either a great deal of forethought or exact improvisation. Regardless, his mental acuity, intentionality, and originality has become refined throughout the history of his career.

# SMURFO: A Whole-Brain Artist
## SMURFO carries within his artistic work in addition to his verbal expression the poise of a philosopher.
To finish our interview, he provided an additional piece of wisdom for the upcoming generations of artists that in many ways defines his own journey. “I would only want to tell the new generation of painters and artists who are doing what they love to do to just stick with it…everybody’s style has to sharpen up. You know you can’t be as rough as you were five years ago, five years later. You’re gonna have to make sure that you are always keeping your work tight. So do not be afraid to improve. Just because you feel like this one aesthetic you have is going to be the thing, and that might counteract me saying, do what you love to do, but I’m saying don’t be afraid to do it even better or to trim the fat.”

Twice a year, the UW Office of Research awards Royalty Research Fund (RRF) grants to faculty who have submitted proposals for research-related projects. Two of our faculty received such grants in January 2019.
April 07, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## For Want of a Nail
3D4M Assistant Professor Michael Swaine is co-author of a new book documenting research that began with a 2014 Futurefarmers artwork responding to New Mexico's complex nuclear history and the Manhattan Project led by Robert Oppenheimer.
April 07, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Bellingham National
The Whatcom Museum is showing _Bellingham National 2019 Juried Art Exhibition and Awards_ through May 19. Painting + Drawing Professor Philip Govedare and three alums have work included. Govedare won the top juror prize!
January 28, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## IxD Students at Cooper Hewitt
Five junior-level students in Interaction Design answered a challenge from Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. Their design was selected and shown at the museum plus they made a presentation there.
April 01, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Cobblestones and Lumber: UW x SFAI
IVA Assistant Professor Whitney Lynn collaborated with a colleague at San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI) to organize a joint exhibition of MFA student work at the SFAI Fort Mason Campus.
April 08, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Zhi LIn Exhibitions
With the 150th anniversary of the golden spike and the creation of the transcontinental railroad taking place in May 2019, Painting + Drawing Professor Lin's research on Chinese railroad workers is being shared in multiple locations.
April 03, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Rodriguez at MadArt + More
George Rodriguez (MFA 2009) joined the School's Advisory Board earlier this year and has a project at MadArt Studio in April and May. He has been receiving growing recognition for his artwork.
April 06, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## 4Culture Collection Additions
At the end of January, 4Culture announced additions to its Portable Works collection for the first time since 2013. Artworks by the late Professor Emeritus Akio Takamori and thirteen alums were included.
February 13, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Donors: April 2018 – March 2019
Gifts from our generous donors — individuals, foundations, and organizations — are critical to the success and morale of the School. We are deeply grateful for their support. Join them by selecting one of our top funds for your donation.
April 09, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Student Stories


# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Q+A with Ortblad
Clare Ortblad will receive her Master of Design degree in June. She answers questions about her background and her experiences as a graduate student in the Division of Design.
April 06, 2019

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Students Respond to Critical Issues
ART 361/561 — Critical Issues in Contemporary Art Practice — is a course taught each winter quarter. Several students from this year's course write about the opportunity to hear and interact with multiple guest artists.
April 08, 2019

Source: https://www.artworkarchive.com/blog/complete-guide-to-2019-artist-grants-opportunities?fbclid=IwAR1ca_Buz94wZMliYHrBW5T5Ya06a1muW4xIv61D9j6QlKdYgiYiIHO5eyU
Title: Complete Guide to 2019 Artist Grants & Opportunities
Chunks: 184,185,186,187,188,189,190,191,192,193,194,195
## **Call for Art: Place Setting**
The Politits: Art Coalition is honored to announce an open call for our 3rd annual juried exhibition. Place Setting is inspired by the idea of the dinner table, a place where artists are welcome to join in conversation, to share, reflect and organize during a time of unrest. Place Setting is focused on supporting artists who have historically been underrepresented in the arts.
**WHO:** Underrepresented artists worldwide
**DATES:** March 1 - 23, 2019
**LOCATION:**Rochester, NY
**DEADLINE:** January 15, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Submission fee: $15 for 1-3 images. This show is for those who are feeling unheard, fed-up, full of rage and are looking for support from their fellow creatives. Learn more here.

## **FRESH, 2019**
FRESH: not previously known or used; new or different. recent, latest, up-to-date, modern, modernistic, ultramodern, newfangled, original, novel, innovative, unusual, unconventional, unorthodox, radical, revolutionary, informal, offbeat. A juried show by SoLA Gallery.
**WHO:**All artists and all media
**DATES:** February 23 – March 30, 2019
**LOCATION:** Los Angeles, CA
**DEADLINE:** January 19, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Art made within the past two years. Opening reception on February 23. Learn more here.

## **Animalistic Call for Art**
Animals. They are our innocents, our beasts, our wild. They are caged, they are hunted, they are tamed, they are dissected, and they are forgiving. In this call for artists, Linus Gallery asks artists to depict the beauty and majesty of our wild beings, animals.
**WHO:** Artists worldwide
**LOCATION:**Long Beach, CA
**DEADLINE:** January 28, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** All art mediums will be considered in this call for submissions, from photography, wall sculpture, ceramics, fabric, mixed media, all paintings and drawings including, oil, acrylic, pastels, ink, graphite, etc. Cost: $35 for 3 entries, $5 for additional entries. Learn more here.

## ****Simpos’ art** Festival**
The cultural association MPGart, a non-profit-making association, promotes and organizes the I edition of the Simpos’art Festival in the town of Vittoria, Italy. The aim is to raise awareness about contemporary art in its different languages.
**WHO:** Artists working in painting, sculpture, photography, installation, art video.
**DATES:** September 14 - October 6, 2019
**LOCATION:** Vittoria, Italy
**DEADLINE:** January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Apply by email. Required: photos for each submitted works in high solution jpg with a complete tagline (title, size and technique), artist biography and telephone number. Learn more here.

## **Neoteric Abstract VII**
This call from Limner Gallery is for a thematic exhibition dedicated to abstract art. The exhibition is open to all forms of abstraction, from the geometric to the lyrical, from the precise to the raw.
**WHO:**All working artists in any media
**DATES:**April 4 – 28, 2019
**LOCATION:** Hudson, NY
**DEADLINE:**January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Entrants must be 18 years of age or older to apply. Wall mounted works must not be taller than 96" no wider than 120". Sculptural work must fit through a standard height, 36"wide entry door. Learn more here.

## **All About Photo Awards 2019**
Our fourth edition of the All About Photo Awards invites photographers from around the world to submit their best work for consideration.
**WHO:** Photographers worldwide, age 18 and older, professional and amateur
**START DATE:** May 1, 2019
**LOCATION:** Pinecrest, FL
**DEADLINE:** January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** $10,000 in cash awards, extensive press coverage and global recognition for winners. $30 (US Dollars) for the 3 first images. $5 (US Dollars) for each additional image. Learn more here.

## **World Illustration Awards 2019**
The Association of Illustrators (AOI) in partnership with USA-based Directory of Illustration, announces that the World Illustration Awards 2019 are now open for entries. Illustrators are invited to submit work made in the 2018 calendar year.
**WHO:** Illustrators, commissioners, agents and tutors worldwide
**LOCATION:** London, ENG
**DEADLINE**: January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Eight award categories: Advertising, Books sponsored by NoBrow, Children’s Books sponsored by Walker Books, Design, Editorial, Experimental, Research and Site Specific. Learn more here.
****

## **February Calls-for-Entry:**


## **2019 St. Joseph Sculpture Walk**
The Allied Arts Council and the City of Saint Joseph, Missouri seek sculptures to be placed in Downtown Saint Joseph. Selected sculptures/sculptors will receive a $500 honorarium and all sculptures selected will be competing for up to $13,000 in cash prize awards.
**WHO:** Regional, national, and international sculpture artists
**DATES:** June 2019 - May 2020
**LOCATION:** Saint Joseph, Missouri
**DEADLINE:** February 1, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** The Allied Arts Council will purchase a sculpture to become a permanent part of Saint Joseph's public art collection. Only pieces priced $15,000 or less will be considered for purchase. Learn more here.

## **Photo 21: Future Forward**
PH GALLERY + STUDIO seeks photo-based artists to participate in the 4th Annual Juried Group Exhibition. PHOTO21 engages with artists whose work actively pushes the boundaries of traditional photographic and visual expression thereby forging new ground in the practice of the photographic medium. What is the future of the photographic object? This exhibition explores this question through the 21st century artists' eyes and mind.
**WHO:** Photographers
**DATES:**March 29, 2019 - May 31, 2019
**LOCATION:** Troy, NY
**DEADLINE:** February 2, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Photo-based works, including film, digital photography, 2-D, 3-D, installation, mixed media, sound and all forms of photo-based media will be considered. Learn more here.

## **Women in Art - 2019**
Las Laguna Gallery is seeking works from women artists. This exhibition is dedicated to the spirit and creativity of all women artists, past and present.
**WHO:** All local, national, and international artists, professional and amateur
**DATES:**March 7 – 29, 2019
**LOCATION:** Laguna Beach, CA
**DEADLINE:** February 4, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Works in Acrylic, Airbrush, Assemblage, Charcoal, Color Pencil, Collage, Digital Art, Drawings, Encaustic, Fiber Art, Graphite, Illustration, Mixed Media, New Media, Oil, Painting, Pastel, Photography (Traditional and Digital), and Watercolor, will be considered. Learn more here.

## **Paper 2019 National Exbition**
PAPER 2019 exhibition features pieces by artists working in paper broadly considered. Submissions may include prints, drawings, photographs, artists’ books, handmade paper as well as three-dimensional works made with paper. The aim of the exhibition is to highlight the vitality, diversity, sense of experimentation and skillful execution and the many ways in which contemporary artists approach this material.
**WHO:** Paper artists
**DATES:** April 7 - May 16, 2019
**LOCATION:** New Canaan, CT
**DEADLINE:**February 7, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Best in Show, awards an artist a solo exhibition at Silvermine Arts Center with a $1,000 stipend for show related expenses. To be considered for the Best in Show Prize, artists are required to enter a minimum of three works. Learn more here.

# Spring 2019 Newsletter
## Director's Notes
On the first day of April, as I was enjoying that glorious rite of spring quarter — walking through The Quad in awe of the cherry blossoms and the vast crowds of fellow admirers — I overheard two couples exclaim…
April 09, 2019

texts.184:
## **Call for Art: Place Setting**
The Politits: Art Coalition is honored to announce an open call for our 3rd annual juried exhibition. Place Setting is inspired by the idea of the dinner table, a place where artists are welcome to join in conversation, to share, reflect and organize during a time of unrest. Place Setting is focused on supporting artists who have historically been underrepresented in the arts.
**WHO:** Underrepresented artists worldwide
**DATES:** March 1 - 23, 2019
**LOCATION:**Rochester, NY
**DEADLINE:** January 15, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Submission fee: $15 for 1-3 images. This show is for those who are feeling unheard, fed-up, full of rage and are looking for support from their fellow creatives. Learn more here.
texts.185:
## **FRESH, 2019**
FRESH: not previously known or used; new or different. recent, latest, up-to-date, modern, modernistic, ultramodern, newfangled, original, novel, innovative, unusual, unconventional, unorthodox, radical, revolutionary, informal, offbeat. A juried show by SoLA Gallery.
**WHO:**All artists and all media
**DATES:** February 23 – March 30, 2019
**LOCATION:** Los Angeles, CA
**DEADLINE:** January 19, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Art made within the past two years. Opening reception on February 23. Learn more here.
texts.186:
## **Animalistic Call for Art**
Animals. They are our innocents, our beasts, our wild. They are caged, they are hunted, they are tamed, they are dissected, and they are forgiving. In this call for artists, Linus Gallery asks artists to depict the beauty and majesty of our wild beings, animals.
**WHO:** Artists worldwide
**LOCATION:**Long Beach, CA
**DEADLINE:** January 28, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** All art mediums will be considered in this call for submissions, from photography, wall sculpture, ceramics, fabric, mixed media, all paintings and drawings including, oil, acrylic, pastels, ink, graphite, etc. Cost: $35 for 3 entries, $5 for additional entries. Learn more here.
texts.187:
## ****Simpos’ art** Festival**
The cultural association MPGart, a non-profit-making association, promotes and organizes the I edition of the Simpos’art Festival in the town of Vittoria, Italy. The aim is to raise awareness about contemporary art in its different languages.
**WHO:** Artists working in painting, sculpture, photography, installation, art video.
**DATES:** September 14 - October 6, 2019
**LOCATION:** Vittoria, Italy
**DEADLINE:** January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Apply by email. Required: photos for each submitted works in high solution jpg with a complete tagline (title, size and technique), artist biography and telephone number. Learn more here.
texts.188:
## **Neoteric Abstract VII**
This call from Limner Gallery is for a thematic exhibition dedicated to abstract art. The exhibition is open to all forms of abstraction, from the geometric to the lyrical, from the precise to the raw.
**WHO:**All working artists in any media
**DATES:**April 4 – 28, 2019
**LOCATION:** Hudson, NY
**DEADLINE:**January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Entrants must be 18 years of age or older to apply. Wall mounted works must not be taller than 96" no wider than 120". Sculptural work must fit through a standard height, 36"wide entry door. Learn more here.
texts.189:
## **All About Photo Awards 2019**
Our fourth edition of the All About Photo Awards invites photographers from around the world to submit their best work for consideration.
**WHO:** Photographers worldwide, age 18 and older, professional and amateur
**START DATE:** May 1, 2019
**LOCATION:** Pinecrest, FL
**DEADLINE:** January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** $10,000 in cash awards, extensive press coverage and global recognition for winners. $30 (US Dollars) for the 3 first images. $5 (US Dollars) for each additional image. Learn more here.
texts.190:
## **World Illustration Awards 2019**
The Association of Illustrators (AOI) in partnership with USA-based Directory of Illustration, announces that the World Illustration Awards 2019 are now open for entries. Illustrators are invited to submit work made in the 2018 calendar year.
**WHO:** Illustrators, commissioners, agents and tutors worldwide
**LOCATION:** London, ENG
**DEADLINE**: January 31, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Eight award categories: Advertising, Books sponsored by NoBrow, Children’s Books sponsored by Walker Books, Design, Editorial, Experimental, Research and Site Specific. Learn more here.
****
texts.192:
## **2019 St. Joseph Sculpture Walk**
The Allied Arts Council and the City of Saint Joseph, Missouri seek sculptures to be placed in Downtown Saint Joseph. Selected sculptures/sculptors will receive a $500 honorarium and all sculptures selected will be competing for up to $13,000 in cash prize awards.
**WHO:** Regional, national, and international sculpture artists
**DATES:** June 2019 - May 2020
**LOCATION:** Saint Joseph, Missouri
**DEADLINE:** February 1, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** The Allied Arts Council will purchase a sculpture to become a permanent part of Saint Joseph's public art collection. Only pieces priced $15,000 or less will be considered for purchase. Learn more here.
texts.193:
## **Photo 21: Future Forward**
PH GALLERY + STUDIO seeks photo-based artists to participate in the 4th Annual Juried Group Exhibition. PHOTO21 engages with artists whose work actively pushes the boundaries of traditional photographic and visual expression thereby forging new ground in the practice of the photographic medium. What is the future of the photographic object? This exhibition explores this question through the 21st century artists' eyes and mind.
**WHO:** Photographers
**DATES:**March 29, 2019 - May 31, 2019
**LOCATION:** Troy, NY
**DEADLINE:** February 2, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Photo-based works, including film, digital photography, 2-D, 3-D, installation, mixed media, sound and all forms of photo-based media will be considered. Learn more here.
texts.194:
## **Women in Art - 2019**
Las Laguna Gallery is seeking works from women artists. This exhibition is dedicated to the spirit and creativity of all women artists, past and present.
**WHO:** All local, national, and international artists, professional and amateur
**DATES:**March 7 – 29, 2019
**LOCATION:** Laguna Beach, CA
**DEADLINE:** February 4, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Works in Acrylic, Airbrush, Assemblage, Charcoal, Color Pencil, Collage, Digital Art, Drawings, Encaustic, Fiber Art, Graphite, Illustration, Mixed Media, New Media, Oil, Painting, Pastel, Photography (Traditional and Digital), and Watercolor, will be considered. Learn more here.
texts.195:
## **Paper 2019 National Exbition**
PAPER 2019 exhibition features pieces by artists working in paper broadly considered. Submissions may include prints, drawings, photographs, artists’ books, handmade paper as well as three-dimensional works made with paper. The aim of the exhibition is to highlight the vitality, diversity, sense of experimentation and skillful execution and the many ways in which contemporary artists approach this material.
**WHO:** Paper artists
**DATES:** April 7 - May 16, 2019
**LOCATION:** New Canaan, CT
**DEADLINE:**February 7, 2019
**FINE PRINT:** Best in Show, awards an artist a solo exhibition at Silvermine Arts Center with a $1,000 stipend for show related expenses. To be considered for the Best in Show Prize, artists are required to enter a minimum of three works. Learn more here.

126 Learn to imitate respectfully, then innovate. Master the fundamentals to make connections nobody else has made. That's true innovation. #ArtEducation #CreativeProcess #Innovation #Imitation #Masterpiece #ArtInspiration #FollowYourArt #LearnAndGrow
850 These are all things I’m actively learning and trying to master. Be patient with me: 1- Listen to your body. I can’t do everything all the time and all at once. My family and friends say I am constantly on the go. Are they right? Yes. Am I still learning to slow down because I can’t sustain working so much? Absolutely. 2- Never be afraid to try new things. I’ve been sitting on ideas and materials for years to the point where it feels silly now. Try the technique. Experiment. Fail. That’s how you grow in the first place. 3- Confidence comes before execution. I may have never done something before but I refuse to let that limit me. Practice, research, and consistency will outweigh talent any day. Remember, there’s a first time for everything. 4- There will be a lot of no’s. I get way more no’s than I do yeses. That’s why it’s important to not compare yourself to others. You’ve no ideas how many no’s they got before they received the right yes. Take it to the chin and move on to the next one. 5- Have fun with it. Like many things, if something doesn’t feel right whether it’s time, energy, spirit or whatever else, listen to that. Creating is work but it should also be fun work. Life is short. Enjoy it while you’re here. #workingartist #professionalartist #contemporaryartist #muralartist #artistjourney

Title: 6.9K views · 353 reactions | About ten strangers want to give $1,000 to the art idea you’ve been sitting on for years.

It’s the Awesome Foundation. Every month, in cities all over the world, groups of about ten people each put $100 of their own money into a pot and hand the whole $1,000 to one idea. No strings, and you never pay it back. They’ve been doing it since 2009.

Anyone can apply. In their words: if you can fill in the form, you can apply. No degree, no CV, no gallery.

Each chapter decides for itself what counts as awesome, and art is one of the things they fund. The mural you’ve sketched a hundred times. Portraits of the people on your street. Free painting classes somewhere that’s never had them. The show you keep saying you’ll put on.

Write it tonight in three sentences:
1. What the project is.
2. Who it’ll delight.
3. Exactly what the $1,000 buys.
Add one picture of your work, and pick the chapter nearest you. Many prefer local projects, though every chapter can see every application.

The honest catches: it’s for a project, not your bills, and each chapter funds one idea a month, so it’s competitive.

That idea has been waiting years for permission. This is ten strangers offering it.

Information without action is just expensive entertainment.

Send this to the artist friend whose idea you’d fund yourself if you could.
