Established in 2017, Circle Foundation for the Arts located in Lyon, France is a private online gallery with a rich handpicked selection of remarkable fine art. Through a variety of formats, they provide an eclectic source for art lovers, collectors and professionals who wish to discover new artists from around the globe.
I entered their competition “Artist of the Month” and while I wasn’t one of the three artists selected to be highlighted on their website and in their monthly magazine I was happy to learn that I was voted “Top in Category for Drawing” based on the five drawings I submitted for their consideration.
Additionally they invited me to be interviewed on their website regarding my approach to drawing, artistic influences, and my thoughts on contemporary art in general. You can read the interview right here.

# About ten strangers want to give $1,000 to the art idea you’ve been sitting on for years. It’s the Awesome Foundation. Every month, in cities all over the world, groups of about ten people each put $100 of their own money into a pot and hand the whole $1,000 to one idea. No strings, and you never pay it back. They’ve been doing it since 2009. Anyone can apply. In their words: if you can fill in the form, you can apply. No degree, no CV, no gallery. Each chapter decides for itself what counts as awesome, and art is one of the things they fund. The mural you’ve sketched a hundred times. Portraits of the people on your street. Free painting classes somewhere that’s never had them. The show you keep saying you’ll put on. Write it tonight in three sentences: 1. What the project is. 2. Who it’ll delight. 3. Exactly what the $1,000 buys. Add one picture of your work, and pick the chapter nearest you. Many prefer local projects, though every chapter can see every application. The honest catches: it’s for a project, not your bills, and each chapter funds one idea a month, so it’s competitive. That idea has been waiting years for permission. This is ten strangers offering it. Information without action is just expensive entertainment. Send this to the artist friend whose idea you’d fund yourself if you could. #ArtistGrants #ArtFunding #ArtProject #ArtistLife #CreativeFlair | Creative Flair | Facebook

Title: 6.9K views · 353 reactions | About ten strangers want to give $1,000 to the art idea you’ve been sitting on for years.

It’s the Awesome Foundation. Every month, in cities all over the world, groups of about ten people each put $100 of their own money into a pot and hand the whole $1,000 to one idea. No strings, and you never pay it back. They’ve been doing it since 2009.

Anyone can apply. In their words: if you can fill in the form, you can apply. No degree, no CV, no gallery.

Each chapter decides for itself what counts as awesome, and art is one of the things they fund. The mural you’ve sketched a hundred times. Portraits of the people on your street. Free painting classes somewhere that’s never had them. The show you keep saying you’ll put on.

Write it tonight in three sentences:
1. What the project is.
2. Who it’ll delight.
3. Exactly what the $1,000 buys.
Add one picture of your work, and pick the chapter nearest you. Many prefer local projects, though every chapter can see every application.

The honest catches: it’s for a project, not your bills, and each chapter funds one idea a month, so it’s competitive.

That idea has been waiting years for permission. This is ten strangers offering it.

Information without action is just expensive entertainment.

Send this to the artist friend whose idea you’d fund yourself if you could.

1,071 A short story about me It’s true—since I was a little girl, I wanted to do hair. I know, I know… “That’s what they all say.” But it’s the truth. My journey started a bit later in life than most. I had my daughter at 19 and my son at 21. I know—insane. I was young and already had a family, so my dream of doing hair was pushed to the back burner. I went through some unimaginable things from 19 until about 23 (but that’s a story for another day). Eventually, things got a little easier, and I finally bit the bullet. I went to school and got licensed in 2012. The environment of doing hair was never easy for me. Honestly, I still have a hard time sometimes. I was never the girl with a lot of girlfriends—just a couple of really close ones. And being in the beauty industry surrounds you with a lot of women. But let me tell you… I can’t imagine myself doing anything else. The constant laughs, the support, the sweet friendships I’ve made, and the confidence I’ve built over the last 14 years make my little-girl heart so happy. So here I am—living the dream of being my own boss, making women feel beautiful, and meeting amazing people along the way.

2,387 Sometimes people see where you are and assume it happened quickly. But the truth almost always is, it didn’t. (And my dear friends who I have tagged will agree!) Stepping into roles where you educate, motivate, and lead isn’t always easy. It requires a commitment to constantly learning, questioning information, and being open minded to relearning. It means showing up for others even on the days when it’s hard for you. It means airport delays are apart of life, hotel pillows are bound to leave you with a stiff neck, and FaceTiming loved ones vs. hugging them good night. It means pushing through the uncomfortable moments, knowing on the other side of the discomfort is growth. It means being selfless time and time again because it’s never been about you, and it’s always been about them. As a person who’s taken on the role of a educator, mentor, and leader, It’s been over 20 years of showing up on ALL of the days — because I care deeply about our community of stylists. Being able to watch others grow, step into their power, and cheer them on is one of the greatest gifts of this career. So if you’re working toward a dream right now, keep going — especially on the hard days. One day you’ll look back and realize those were the moments that have helped built everything you’ve dreamed of. And I promise, you (and the people around you) will be so proud! ✨

892 We love this industry… but let’s be honest, it doesn’t always love us back. Most of us came into this career full of passion — excited to create, connect, and build something meaningful. But somewhere along the way, we were handed “norms” that left us overworked, underpaid, burnt out, and questioning why we started in the first place. The truth? A lot of the traditional paths in this industry weren’t built to benefit stylists… they were built to keep us small, busy, and dependent. But here’s the good news — we don’t have to follow them. There are ways to take back your passion. Ways to build income that doesn’t rely on constant burnout. Ways to grow without competing, gossiping, or playing into the toxicity. Ways to make this career actually work for you. To the stylist doing it differently… keep going. You’re not breaking the industry — you’re helping rebuild it. ✨ #beyondthechair #hairstylist #stylistlife
1,679 this past month feels like something i used to only daydream about… in the middle of my busiest season behind the chair, i somehow found myself learning, growing, traveling, creating, and still making space to love on the people who matter most to me. and that balance? that’s something i don’t take lightly. getting to be mentored by jacob kahn at creator con lit a fire in me i didn’t even know was possible. assisting morgan at the be well nyc show pushed me, inspired me, and reminded me why i fell in love with this industry in the first place. meeting so many people I look up to and also motivate me has been such an insane fuel to these wild dreams and then coming home to my clients, my people, my routines… it made everything feel real. like my dreams aren’t just dreams anymore, they’re happening in real time. i feel so grateful. like deeply, overwhelmingly grateful. and i have to say… doing all of this alongside nikki, my literal dream weaver, makes it even more special. I wouldn’t have these opportunities if it wasn’t for bloom. her dreams motivate my dreams. the way we build, push, and believe in each other is something i’ll never take for granted. this month stretched me in the best way. and for the first time, the life i’ve been working toward feels tangible. more please 🖤

**Copyright © 2018 All rights reserved**
JOIN OUR MAILING LIST
Brenda Pinkston is a dynamic artist who discovered her
natural gift for transforming visions into expressive art
at an early age. She attributes her creativity to her
Creator and credits her mother for nurturing her artistic
development. As a child, she quickly traded coloring
books for sketchpads, pencils, brushes, and watercolors,
fully immersing herself in the world of art. Her passion
led her to pursue formal training, earning a Bachelor of
Fine Arts degree from The College of New Jersey.
Brenda began her career as a commercial artist, developing fashion ad campaigns for a specialty designer shop, serving as an art editor for a local newspaper, illustrating published children’s books, and later working as a computer programmer and web developer for the State of New Jersey.
Her journey took an unexpected turn when she was involved in two auto accidents that profoundly impacted her life. Facing numerous medical challenges, she developed a deeper connection to art. Through perseverance and multiple surgeries, she transformed her pain into triumph, regaining her ability to draw and paint.
Today, Brenda’s artwork is nationally recognized, adorning homes and institutions across America. Though a New Jersey native, she now creates new works from her art studio gallery in Charlotte, North Carolina.​

Artist Statement
My work captures the essence of the
human experience—our relationships,
interactions, and the emotional
currents they create, both positive
and the uncomfortable. This dynamic
serves as the foundation of my artistic
exploration. I have always been
fascinated by human behavior, particularly those profound moments—big or small—that shape our lives.
In my paintings, I strive for more than storytelling. I aim to reveal the emotions behind the story. Each of us is unique, yet we all navigate a spectrum of emotions deeply tied to our personal journeys. When you stand before my work and allow your eyes to glide across the infinite brushstrokes, you may find the narrative—though from my perspective—feels familiar. It may bring you peace, make you smile, laugh, raise awareness, disrupt patterns, shift perspectives, and contribute to healing social trauma. Ultimately, my goal is to stir emotions that foster personal reflection and social expansion within our communities.
I am drawn to large-scale, expressive paintings that allow my impressionist-influenced style to flow freely, amplifying the emotional depth of each piece. My brushstrokes are like music—soulful, rhythmic movements that electrify the canvas with life and motion.
At the heart of my work is an unapologetic celebration of the African American experience—its love, joy, resilience, and healing, as well as the unique nuances of family life. I am deeply committed to visually preserving and sharing these stories, understanding the power of imagery in defining and honoring cultural identity. My purpose as an artist is clear: I was born to translate this experience onto canvas, ensuring it is seen, felt, and remembered.

## Dark, funny, and off-kilter stories about the moving parts to being human.
_“Lana Pesch’s stories have one foot in the world of Alice Munro –long, deep, satisfying and unsettling in equal measure–and the other foot in a younger, jazzier world where humour is currency and the sentence is king.”_
—_Annabel Lyon, author of_ The Golden Mean _and_ The Sweet Girl
_“This is a boffo collection. Lana Pesch writes with intelligence, humour, and compassion. Her stories show the brokenness of being human, but with lightness and verve.”_
—_Sarah Selecky, author of_ This Cake Is for the Party
_“Witty, moving, urbane, and thoroughly modern, Moving Parts is a knockout collection. A hip cross-country tour of today’s North America.”_
—_Arjun Basu, author of_ Waiting for the Man
Video 3

A blind date blooms in a grocery store parking lot. Lake Erie forms the backdrop to a botched assisted suicide. A plane crash on the BC coast brings a frustrated artist and hardened bootlegger together in a dire situation. These flawed, often broken characters seek meaning, acceptance, and closure under extraordinary circumstances ... though not necessarily in that order.
Insightful and heartbreaking–with the occasional sharp turn towards the surreal–_Moving Parts_ is a collection of deeply imagined, darkly funny short stories. Pesch’s writing is surprising, charming, and unsettling. Her characters are raw and inappropriate, loving and confrontational and completely recognizable.

**Q & A with author Lana Pesch**
_“I am fascinated by human behavior–the extremes of both good and bad, and the spectrum in between. We are a flawed species, in my opinion. Always making mistakes. But we learn by failing.”_
**Q: Let’s talk about the short story form. How should short stories work?**
A story should leave you affected somehow, itchy, shocked, enlightened, comforted, wondering, maybe in a state of self-reflection. They should resonate, linger, and stay with a reader after the book has been put away. Stories should make us wonder and question, and hopefully, shape us into becoming more compassionate human beings. A good story should make you feel less alone. As readers, we might recognize ourselves in a story, we might learn something, or be changed in some way–large or small.

## Dark, funny, and off-kilter stories about the moving parts to being human.
I think stories matter, ultimately, for that connection between writer and reader. For me, both reading and writing are ways to process things I find difficult, absurd, unfair, sorrowful. Stories are a way to enjoy and celebrate language, to have a laugh, employ empathy. Ordinary subjects matter. Alice Munro writes, “The complexity of thing–the things within things–just seems to be endless. I mean nothing is easy, nothing is simple.”
Stories should convey human emotion through language. Ben Marcus also writes, “…language is the true code of our inner lives, and to be a story writer is to know this, to tap into and reveal those ways of personal address we reserve for the private, necessary messages we send ourselves, when we think no one is listening.” Good grief, yes! Because the fact is, somebody _is_ listening.
To quote Thomas King, “The truth about stories is that is all we are.”
**Q: How long have you been working on this collection?**
I’ve been working on this collection since 2008. The first story I had critiqued was “Habits of Creatures.” It looked different back then. I never set out to write a book, but after a while the stories started to pile up so I called Sarah Selecky and said, “Now what?” And she told me I had written a collection. It sounds simple, but it wasn’t. It was a lot of work. A lot of pushing through a lot of resistance.
**Q: What is your writing process like?**
I write all my first drafts by hand. Long form, in a notebook. I would have never done this six years ago, but now I can’t do it any other way. Eventually I transcribe the work to a computer. Then come the revisions. Lots and lots and lots of revisions. I am a chronic tinkerer.
I prefer to write in the morning when my mind is clearer, more open, and there’s less clutter, less distraction.

It’s so funny you said it because Jay Williams and I were his conversation earlier. Even when I say, I’m an organizational psychologist. ### Connection Between Creativity And Organizational Psychology
**One of the reoccurring themes I hear is creativity from starting out to being a hairdresser to whether it’s going into business for yourself, working with other creatives for somebody like Sebastian. What I realized was, the passion and everything around Fashion Week and I know a lot of hairdressers reading this and creative people will go, “When I see this,” but you can be as creative as you want. You go on social media and I just scroll.

### Connection Between Creativity And Organizational Psychology

How are they getting everyone in this room to drink the Kool-Aid?” I fascinated by this.
I began to become very fascinated and what I realized was I was fascinated by human behavior. It all circled back to the darn psychology degree that I got and that there’s creativity to it. I leave you with this on this topic. What blew my mind and what shifted my thinking is what I was playing with the idea of going to graduate school. texts.0: 1,071 A short story about me It’s true—since I was a little girl, I wanted to do hair. I know, I know… “That’s what they all say.” But it’s the truth. My journey started a bit later in life than most. I had my daughter at 19 and my son at 21. I know—insane. I was young and already had a family, so my dream of doing hair was pushed to the back burner. I went through some unimaginable things from 19 until about 23 (but that’s a story for another day). Eventually, things got a little easier, and I finally bit the bullet. I went to school and got licensed in 2012. The environment of doing hair was never easy for me. Honestly, I still have a hard time sometimes. I was never the girl with a lot of girlfriends—just a couple of really close ones. And being in the beauty industry surrounds you with a lot of women. But let me tell you… I can’t imagine myself doing anything else. The constant laughs, the support, the sweet friendships I’ve made, and the confidence I’ve built over the last 14 years make my little-girl heart so happy. So here I am—living the dream of being my own boss, making women feel beautiful, and meeting amazing people along the way.
texts.1: 2,387 Sometimes people see where you are and assume it happened quickly. But the truth almost always is, it didn’t. (And my dear friends who I have tagged will agree!) Stepping into roles where you educate, motivate, and lead isn’t always easy. It requires a commitment to constantly learning, questioning information, and being open minded to relearning. It means showing up for others even on the days when it’s hard for you. It means airport delays are apart of life, hotel pillows are bound to leave you with a stiff neck, and FaceTiming loved ones vs. hugging them good night. It means pushing through the uncomfortable moments, knowing on the other side of the discomfort is growth. It means being selfless time and time again because it’s never been about you, and it’s always been about them. As a person who’s taken on the role of a educator, mentor, and leader, It’s been over 20 years of showing up on ALL of the days — because I care deeply about our community of stylists. Being able to watch others grow, step into their power, and cheer them on is one of the greatest gifts of this career. So if you’re working toward a dream right now, keep going — especially on the hard days. One day you’ll look back and realize those were the moments that have helped built everything you’ve dreamed of. And I promise, you (and the people around you) will be so proud! ✨

892 We love this industry… but let’s be honest, it doesn’t always love us back. Most of us came into this career full of passion — excited to create, connect, and build something meaningful. But somewhere along the way, we were handed “norms” that left us overworked, underpaid, burnt out, and questioning why we started in the first place. The truth? A lot of the traditional paths in this industry weren’t built to benefit stylists… they were built to keep us small, busy, and dependent. But here’s the good news — we don’t have to follow them. There are ways to take back your passion. Ways to build income that doesn’t rely on constant burnout. Ways to grow without competing, gossiping, or playing into the toxicity. Ways to make this career actually work for you. To the stylist doing it differently… keep going. You’re not breaking the industry — you’re helping rebuild it. ✨ #beyondthechair #hairstylist #stylistlife
1,679 this past month feels like something i used to only daydream about… in the middle of my busiest season behind the chair, i somehow found myself learning, growing, traveling, creating, and still making space to love on the people who matter most to me. and that balance? that’s something i don’t take lightly. getting to be mentored by jacob kahn at creator con lit a fire in me i didn’t even know was possible. assisting morgan at the be well nyc show pushed me, inspired me, and reminded me why i fell in love with this industry in the first place. meeting so many people I look up to and also motivate me has been such an insane fuel to these wild dreams and then coming home to my clients, my people, my routines… it made everything feel real. like my dreams aren’t just dreams anymore, they’re happening in real time. i feel so grateful. like deeply, overwhelmingly grateful. and i have to say… doing all of this alongside nikki, my literal dream weaver, makes it even more special. I wouldn’t have these opportunities if it wasn’t for bloom. her dreams motivate my dreams. the way we build, push, and believe in each other is something i’ll never take for granted. this month stretched me in the best way. and for the first time, the life i’ve been working toward feels tangible. more please 🖤

Brenda Pinkston is a dynamic artist who discovered her
natural gift for transforming visions into expressive art
at an early age. She attributes her creativity to her
Creator and credits her mother for nurturing her artistic
development. As a child, she quickly traded coloring
books for sketchpads, pencils, brushes, and watercolors,
fully immersing herself in the world of art. Her passion
led her to pursue formal training, earning a Bachelor of
Fine Arts degree from The College of New Jersey.
Brenda began her career as a commercial artist, developing fashion ad campaigns for a specialty designer shop, serving as an art editor for a local newspaper, illustrating published children’s books, and later working as a computer programmer and web developer for the State of New Jersey.
Her journey took an unexpected turn when she was involved in two auto accidents that profoundly impacted her life. Facing numerous medical challenges, she developed a deeper connection to art. Through perseverance and multiple surgeries, she transformed her pain into triumph, regaining her ability to draw and paint.
Today, Brenda’s artwork is nationally recognized, adorning homes and institutions across America. Though a New Jersey native, she now creates new works from her art studio gallery in Charlotte, North Carolina.​

Artist Statement
My work captures the essence of the
human experience—our relationships,
interactions, and the emotional
currents they create, both positive
and the uncomfortable. This dynamic
serves as the foundation of my artistic
exploration. I have always been
fascinated by human behavior, particularly those profound moments—big or small—that shape our lives.
In my paintings, I strive for more than storytelling. I aim to reveal the emotions behind the story. Each of us is unique, yet we all navigate a spectrum of emotions deeply tied to our personal journeys. When you stand before my work and allow your eyes to glide across the infinite brushstrokes, you may find the narrative—though from my perspective—feels familiar. It may bring you peace, make you smile, laugh, raise awareness, disrupt patterns, shift perspectives, and contribute to healing social trauma. Ultimately, my goal is to stir emotions that foster personal reflection and social expansion within our communities.
I am drawn to large-scale, expressive paintings that allow my impressionist-influenced style to flow freely, amplifying the emotional depth of each piece. My brushstrokes are like music—soulful, rhythmic movements that electrify the canvas with life and motion.
At the heart of my work is an unapologetic celebration of the African American experience—its love, joy, resilience, and healing, as well as the unique nuances of family life. I am deeply committed to visually preserving and sharing these stories, understanding the power of imagery in defining and honoring cultural identity. My purpose as an artist is clear: I was born to translate this experience onto canvas, ensuring it is seen, felt, and remembered.

Because the fact is, somebody _is_ listening.
To quote Thomas King, “The truth about stories is that is all we are.”
**Q: How long have you been working on this collection?**
I’ve been working on this collection since 2008. The first story I had critiqued was “Habits of Creatures.” It looked different back then. I never set out to write a book, but after a while the stories started to pile up so I called Sarah Selecky and said, “Now what?” And she told me I had written a collection. It sounds simple, but it wasn’t. It was a lot of work. A lot of pushing through a lot of resistance.
**Q: What is your writing process like?**
I write all my first drafts by hand. Long form, in a notebook. I would have never done this six years ago, but now I can’t do it any other way. Eventually I transcribe the work to a computer. Then come the revisions. Lots and lots and lots of revisions. I am a chronic tinkerer.
I prefer to write in the morning when my mind is clearer, more open, and there’s less clutter, less distraction.

**Q & A with author Lana Pesch**
_“I am fascinated by human behavior–the extremes of both good and bad, and the spectrum in between. We are a flawed species, in my opinion. Always making mistakes. But we learn by failing.”_
**Q: Let’s talk about the short story form. How should short stories work?**
A story should leave you affected somehow, itchy, shocked, enlightened, comforted, wondering, maybe in a state of self-reflection. They should resonate, linger, and stay with a reader after the book has been put away. Stories should make us wonder and question, and hopefully, shape us into becoming more compassionate human beings. A good story should make you feel less alone. As readers, we might recognize ourselves in a story, we might learn something, or be changed in some way–large or small.

## Dark, funny, and off-kilter stories about the moving parts to being human.
I think stories matter, ultimately, for that connection between writer and reader. For me, both reading and writing are ways to process things I find difficult, absurd, unfair, sorrowful. Stories are a way to enjoy and celebrate language, to have a laugh, employ empathy. Ordinary subjects matter. Alice Munro writes, “The complexity of thing–the things within things–just seems to be endless. I mean nothing is easy, nothing is simple.”
Stories should convey human emotion through language. Ben Marcus also writes, “…language is the true code of our inner lives, and to be a story writer is to know this, to tap into and reveal those ways of personal address we reserve for the private, necessary messages we send ourselves, when we think no one is listening.” Good grief, yes! Because the fact is, somebody _is_ listening.
To quote Thomas King, “The truth about stories is that is all we are.”
**Q: How long have you been working on this collection?**
I’ve been working on this collection since 2008. The first story I had critiqued was “Habits of Creatures.” It looked different back then. I never set out to write a book, but after a while the stories started to pile up so I called Sarah Selecky and said, “Now what?” And she told me I had written a collection. It sounds simple, but it wasn’t. It was a lot of work. A lot of pushing through a lot of resistance.
**Q: What is your writing process like?**
I write all my first drafts by hand. Long form, in a notebook. I would have never done this six years ago, but now I can’t do it any other way. Eventually I transcribe the work to a computer. Then come the revisions. Lots and lots and lots of revisions. I am a chronic tinkerer.
I prefer to write in the morning when my mind is clearer, more open, and there’s less clutter, less distraction.
